technique: line breaks — where the breath falls, and what the break withholds for a beat
lesson:
Today we work on one technique: the line break. A line break is where a line of poem stops and your eye and voice pause before the next line starts. The pause makes you wait a beat before you get the next word, and that wait changes what you notice.

Look at where this poem breaks. "A jay works the cracked oak at the field's edge, loud" stops on "loud," so you hold that word before you learn what it means. "The day won't crack itself open while you lean here—" stops on a dash, so you hang there with nothing finished. The break holds back the next word for one beat. That short wait makes the held word stronger, because you sit with it alone before the line moves on.

Try this: end a line on a word you want the listener to keep in their ear, not on a small word like "the."

The second time through, listen for how long the dash before "So — up!" makes you wait.

Here is the poem.
poem:
A jay works the cracked oak at the field's edge, loud
about it, hammering an acorn held under one black foot,
splitting the shell for the meat with a patience
that doesn't sound like patience at all—all racket
and sideways eye, taking what it came for and no more.
You stand a minute with the cold in your collar
and watch the thing get done the plain way,
one blow and then the next, nobody keeping score.
The hills have gone the rust-and-iron color they take on
before the real cold, and somewhere down the valley
a dog is answering a dog. Enough of the window.
The day won't crack itself open while you lean here—

There are rooms out there full of people learning the same old steps for the first time—

So — up!
